name: Spring Security 6/7 authorization extension points for OPA
description: Spring Security has no native ABAC; integrate OPA via its extension points: (1) custom AuthorizationManager<RequestAuthorizationContext> for HTTP request-level checks; (2) AuthorizationManager<MethodInvocation> for method-level pre-auth (wire as an AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor @Bean Advisor); (3) custom annotation @OpaPreAuthorize(action) for declarative type-safe checks; (4) custom beans callable from SpEL. Spring Security 7.0 renamed AuthorizationManager.check() to authorize(). Build as a standalone starter — the Spring team's recommended pattern; ABAC-in-core was declined (issue #4276).

name: Pluggable claim extractor: JWT -> AbacContext.Subject
description: Don't hardcode token/claim shapes. Define an extractor interface (Authentication -> AbacContext) and ship a default JWT implementation, letting consumers override claim mapping (roles claim, attribute claims). Keeps the library usable with any IdP (Keycloak, Okta, custom) instead of one provider's claim names.

name: Pre-authorization decorator that also removes a redundant resource load
description: Pre-fetch the resource being authorized once, run the ABAC check against it, cache it request-scoped, and let the handler reuse the cached resource instead of re-SELECTing it. This both centralizes the check and removes one DB read per authorized request. Make it opt-in/flag-guarded per handler so behavior is byte-identical when off (handler falls back to its own load+check), enabling gradual rollout.

content: Auto-configuration must be conditional and overridable: gate beans on @ConditionalOnClass / @ConditionalOnProperty, and every bean with @ConditionalOnMissingBean so consumers can replace it. Bind config via @ConfigurationProperties with safe defaults. Register via META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports.

description: The @OpaPreAuthorize pointcut used AnnotationMatchingPointcut.forMethodAnnotation (checkInherited=false), so an annotation declared on an INTERFACE method was never matched under class-based (CGLIB) proxies — Spring Boot's default. The method ran with no enforcement and no error: the worst authz failure mode (looks protected, isn't). The manager's own findAnnotation searched interfaces, masking the gap in any test that exercised the manager directly instead of the pointcut.
resolution: Use new AnnotationMatchingPointcut(null, Annotation.class, true) — checkInherited=true searches the type hierarchy, same posture as Spring Security's own @PreAuthorize pointcut. Pin with a slice test that proxies with setProxyTargetClass(true) and annotates only the interface method. General rule: any custom method-security pointcut must be tested under CGLIB with interface-declared annotations.

title: Generalize fetch-authorize-cache as AbacResourceResolver SPI + request cache; do not port a central class-keyed rule registry
rationale: A central registry presupposes a uniquely-typed command object per operation (a mediator) for total, type-safe class->rule lookup. Vanilla Spring MVC's dispatch unit is the controller method, so a registry degrades to method-name/pointcut keys: runtime-only binding, two sources of truth, no compile-time link. Co-located @OpaPreAuthorize annotations ARE the rule table; the SPI supplies what they lack (resolved instance attributes).

description: spring-boot-starter-opa-abac example-user-management; fixed f453e12; found by retro-audit 2026-06-12.
resolution: Three-part fix: (1) privileged codes are unassignable through general endpoints (single-owner invariant routes through a dedicated transfer flow that atomically downgrades), (2) the guard compares the capability ladder in addition to resource permissions (SubsetGuard.requireAssignableByActor), (3) sweep the MIRROR operations (demote/strip the owner) in the same pass.

name: Starter-shipped @RestControllerAdvice must be standalone, never a subclass of the shared advice base
description: When a starter auto-registers an exception-mapping @RestControllerAdvice (e.g. PersistenceConflictProblemAdvice mapping OptimisticLockingFailureException/DataIntegrityViolationException -> 409 STATE_CONFLICT problem+json), do NOT extend the shared AbstractProblemAdvice base the applications also extend: the subclass would inherit the base's @ExceptionHandler methods (AccessDeniedException etc.), and cross-advice handler resolution in ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver is order-dependent — the starter's inherited handler could silently shadow (or be shadowed by) every service's own advice for those exceptions. Standalone advice + its own ProblemDetailFactory produces the identical body shape with zero ambiguity; @ConditionalOnClass(name=...) string-guards the dao types for non-JPA adopters, @ConditionalOnMissingBean keeps it overridable. Same body shape, disjoint handler sets.

name: Base-scope SPI is fail-closed-to-empty (no throw), unlike the tri-state role supplier
description: GovernedScopeResolver (opa-abac-spring-data) supplies a list's BASE SCOPE: <T extends AbacDataObject> Specification<T> governedScope(subject, resourceType). Its failure posture DIFFERS from HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier's B2 tri-state-throw: because it produces the base scope of a LIST, the only safe failure value is the empty list, so EVERY non-affirmative outcome (empty array, non-200, blank/malformed body, non-UUID element, transport/timeout/connection-refused, null subject) collapses to a shared static denyAll() = (root,q,cb)->cb.disjunction() (an empty OR = always-false = selects no rows) with NO THROW. A throw would 500 the list instead of emptying it; a transport outage yields the SAME empty page as 'governs nothing' — never the whole table. Contrast mx-a55040 (tri-state supplier: outage THROWS so the consumer can distinguish outage from no-role) — there the consumer maps to its own fail-closed; here the SPI IS the fail-closed sink. The catalog impl HttpGovernedScopeResolver mirrors HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier (JDK HttpClient+Jackson, @ConditionalOnProperty(catalog.role-source=http), catalog.user-service.* coords) and calls GET /internal/governed-targets?subject&resourceType -> ["uuid",...] -> root.get("id").in(ids). UNIT-TEST TECHNIQUE for a Specification-returning component without a DB: invoke spec.toPredicate against a MOCKED CriteriaBuilder/Root and assert which predicate it builds — root.get("id").in(Collection) (governed) vs cb.disjunction() (deny-all); the in() overload that fires for a List arg is in(Collection), so stub any(Collection.class), NOT the varargs/Iterable. Consumer (CatalogListAuthorizer) lands in T4; bean is conditional so the demo profile gets none -> ObjectProvider absent -> empty page.

title: Missing id behind an annotated resourceId answers 403 (gate deny), wrong-scope-but-existing keeps the handler's 404
rationale: ADR 0013's literal fail-closed rule (resolver empty/throws -> DENY) re-types not-found from 404 to 403 on every annotated id'd endpoint once a resolver is registered — pinned as anti-enumeration posture rather than special-cased, because any 'empty -> let the handler 404' carve-out would rebuild the attribute-less context path the rule exists to forbid. The 403/404 split is NOT an existence oracle: the wrong-scope 404 is only reachable by callers the policy already ALLOWED for the resource. Operationally: CRUD/error-contract ITs run on the kill-switch off-profile (doubling as the baseline proof); exactly one e2e cell suite-wide (catalog-e2e get-after-delete) flipped 404->403 and was re-pinned in place. General lesson: a slice that moves a decision earlier in the request lifecycle must sweep the status-code contract of every path it now preempts.

title: B2 supplier-outage: outage error-distinct from no-role at the RoleDefinitionSupplier SPI (design settled)
rationale: Grill-me 2026-06-15 settled the B2 phase-① design (ADR 0014 + B2-SUPPLIER-OUTAGE/00-DESIGN). The fix for the one widening-on-failure path (PERMISSION-CATEGORIES-REVIEW C1/C4, aggravated by 6.5): a TRI-STATE RoleDefinitionSupplier contract — Optional.of=resolved; Optional.empty()=authoritative no-role (KEEP, designed realm-fallback signal); THROW RoleResolutionException=outage (deny/no-widening). Pins: (1) unchecked RoleResolutionException in opa-abac-core (family-consistent w/ AncestorResolutionException; keeps @FunctionalInterface lambdas working); (2) STRICT HTTP invariant in HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier — ONLY 204->empty/fallback, ONLY 200+valid->resolved, EVERYTHING ELSE THROWS (200-blank, all 4xx, 5xx, timeout, refused, malformed-200); (3) supplier-classifies/consumer-maps, NO library wrapper (a wrapper either re-introduces the bug or is ceremony; 'deny' is non-uniform across consumers); (4) per-consumer mapping across ALL 5 lookup() consumers — gate managers (OpaPreAuthorize/OpaAuthorizationManager)->explicit catch->403 (the only widening path; rest have no fallback), HierarchicalAuthorizer->catch->false, SubtreeSpecResolver->NO CODE CHANGE (existing catch already collapses; test-only), CategoryListAuthorizer->catch->Page.empty(); (5) NO kill-switch (off-ramp would BE the vuln — consciously breaks the house pattern); (6) ZERO Rego — fallback clause RETAINED (load-bearing for non-members/type-level creates per 5.97); outage denies before any OPA call; opa test 157/157 unchanged; (7) TeamRoleDefinitionSupplier minimal touch (catch DataAccessException->throw, contract-conformant showcase; outcome unchanged, no fallback in user-mgmt); (8) logging WARN at supplier throw-site / DEBUG at consumer catches, no PII (uniform-403 means server log is the only operator outage signal); (9) resilience (retry/circuit-break) OUT of scope -> new Slice B3 (all cross-service HTTP edges: HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier+TagDefinitionClient+OpaClient), sequenced B2->6.7->Phase6->B3->Phase7. Headline proof: IT — realm catalog-editor + mock-supplier-throws (outage) + id'd write the resolved role narrows -> 403 NOT widened fallback (the C1/C4 cut). Ready for /decompose.

name: B3-preserving edge wrapper: retry the transient subset BEFORE B2's throw, one retryable signal per edge (T3)
description: Wrapping an app HTTP edge (HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier resolve, TagDefinitionClient tag) with a CallGuard while preserving B2's strict classification EXACTLY. The discipline: retry only slots AHEAD of the existing fail-closed throw — it never replaces a throw with a fallback. Mechanism: extract the single HTTP exchange + B2 classification into a body method (exchangeAndClassify/exchangeAndParse) that (a) RETURNS for the terminal success signals (204→empty, 200+valid→resolved/definitions) — un-retried; (b) throws the DOMAIN fail-closed exception (RoleResolutionException / TagDefinitionFetchException) straight for a PERMANENT failure (every 4xx, 200-blank, malformed-200) — the guard's error predicate does NOT match it → re-thrown at once, no retry; (c) throws ONE retryable carrier (TransientResolveException / TransientTagException) for the WHOLE transient subset (5xx/429, timeout, connection-refused — transport IOExceptions are caught and re-thrown AS the carrier so no raw IOException escapes the body). The guard's error predicate is then a clean  (do NOT also OR in RetryableClassification.isRetryableError — it's dead since the body emits exactly one retryable type; ORing it in is misleading). lookup/fetchApplicable catch the EXHAUSTED carrier → map back to the domain exception (B2's outcome) and catch CallNotPermittedException (open breaker) → same domain exception (fail closed exactly like an exhausted outage, ADR 0017 §5). PROOF that B2 is intact = ATTEMPT-COUNT assertions via the in-process HttpServer stub: 204/200-valid = exactly 1 attempt (terminal, not retried), 4xx = exactly 1 attempt (permanent, no retry), exhausting 5xx = maxRetries+1 attempts then the domain throw, transient-then-200 recovers. SPRING GOTCHA: adding a 4-arg (…, CallGuard) production constructor alongside the existing 3-arg test/demo ctor gives a @Component TWO public constructors → 'No default constructor found / ambiguous' at context load; fix with @Autowired on the production ctor (the 3-arg one, which builds a CallGuards.disabled(name) single-attempt guard, stays for the existing unit tests so they're byte-identical to pre-B3). Wire resolveCallGuard/tagCallGuard beans in a @Configuration from OpaAbacProperties.getResilience().getResolve()/getTag().toConfig(master) — independent per-endpoint breakers. No-lock invariant holds: both edges run on the request thread, TagAssignmentService is NOT @Transactional. Pinned by ADR 0017 §3; preserves ADR 0014 (B2). Relates to mx-ca8979 (the strict HTTP classification this wraps).

name: ABAC input model: Subject/Action/Resource/Environment
description: Model the OPA decision input as four parts — Subject (who: id, roles, attributes), Action (what: a string verb), Resource (on what: type, id, attributes), Environment (circumstances: map). Keep this record framework-agnostic in opa-abac-core so the Spring modules and any client serialize the same shape as OPA 'input'. Pluggable extraction (JWT claims -> Subject) lives in the spring-security module, never in core.

ROLE_INFRASTRUCTURE method-security advisors that inject their AuthorizationManager DIRECTLY get instantiated during BeanPostProcessor registration (AOP advisor discovery), dragging the manager's whole collaborator graph (RoleDefinitionSupplier, OpaClient, ResourceResolutionSupport) into existence BEFORE user-declared BPPs register — so the GATE's references silently skip every bean-level decorator (B3 ResilientOpaClient, ADR-0023 memos) while later consumers get wrapped beans: one request, two supplier identities. Symptom chain: a counting IT measures N calls instead of 1 + BeanPostProcessorChecker WARN naming the supplier bean as created during BPP [someDecorator] registration. Two follow-on gotchas the newly-effective wrap exposes: (1) ResilientOpaClient deliberately retries the fail-closed false sentinel — a gate DENY now makes 2 OPA hops, so any test pinning decision-dispatch counts must run opa.abac.resilience.opa.enabled=false; (2) MockMvc leaves ServletRequestAttributes bound after perform() BY DESIGN, so a later same-thread DIRECT resolver call in another IT hits the request memo's stale snapshot — reset attributes in @BeforeEach for suites asserting post-mutation reads outside requests.
resolution: Defer the manager: inject ObjectProvider<Manager> into the advisor @Bean and wrap in a tiny AuthorizationManager that SingletonSupplier-drains it on the FIRST DECISION (the idiom Spring Security's own method-security config uses). The manager is then created post-refresh and post-processed by ALL BPPs. Fixed in OpaMethodSecurityConfiguration (7.3 T2); also retro-activates B3's OPA-edge wrap on the gate path.

title: Library-spine authorization is role-definition-driven, via a pluggable RoleDefinitionSupplier SPI
rationale: Generalizing the source platform's proven model: the OPA decision is driven primarily by the caller's role definition (code + attributes + permissions{resourceType:[verbs]}), with JWT tags as an override - NOT by raw token roles. Build RoleDefinition + RoleDefinitionSupplier as first-class core types NOW (with a NoOp default), ship a static DemoRoleDefinitionSupplier in the catalog app, and defer the HTTP-backed supplier (calling the user-management-service) to Phase 4 - a single-bean swap. This avoids reworking the OPA input / annotation / rego wire contract when the user-service lands, because the SPI isolates only the SOURCE of role definitions. Decided over (a) raw-roles-only now and (b) building the user-service first. Planned in docs/to-do/planning/LIBRARY-SPINE.

title: Pre-publish API polish: AbacResource rename + the Taggable.TAGS_ATTRIBUTE contract
rationale: Two public-API fixes found by consuming the starter as an external dependency (Java 25 / SB4 microservice, 2026-07-08), landed together before the first Maven Central publish while breaking changes are still free. (1) AbacDataObject -> AbacResource: the interface names the ROLE in the authz query (input.resource; siblings AbacResourceResolver/AbacResourceCache) — NOT SecuredObject, since most implementers are throwaway resolved views, not persistent secured things. (2) The data-filter's tags attribute name is now a contract constant (Taggable.TAGS_ATTRIBUTE) instead of a hardcoded literal at two sites — a BYO entity maps any DB COLUMN but keeps the JPA ATTRIBUTE name 'tags'; ByoEntityFilterIT pins the contract (interfaces-only entity, custom_tags column, residual + deny-override both proven). Escape hatch if ever needed: an opa.abac.data.tags-attribute property, not an SPI. First-publish release notes must mention both.

name: B2 supplier-outage: the 5 lookup() consumers an SPI change must sweep
description: The B2 fix (distinguish resolve OUTAGE->deny from authoritative NO-ROLE->fallback) is an SPI-contract change on RoleDefinitionSupplier.lookup(). It is NOT one-file: lookup() has 5 PRODUCTION consumers, all collapsing Optional.empty() via .orElse(null) so outage==no-role today: (1) OpaPreAuthorizeAuthorizationManager:119 (spring-security), (2) OpaAuthorizationManager:69 (spring-security), (3) HierarchicalAuthorizer:85 (spring-data), (4) SubtreeSpecResolver:104 (spring-data), (5) CategoryListAuthorizer:85 (catalog example). Plus 3 implementors: NoOpRoleDefinitionSupplier, DemoRoleDefinitionSupplier, HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier (the outage source); and the user-mgmt TeamRoleDefinitionSupplier. The rego seam is has_role_definition (= input.role_definition.permissions present) gating the realm fallback in catalog/category/product.rego. Any consumer left on old semantics = silent residual widening hole. This is the PERMISSION-CATEGORIES-REVIEW lesson ('the sweep stopped at the surface the ticket named') applied pre-emptively. The split-fail-closed precedent to mirror is ADR 0013 section 3 (instance-resolution deny vs ancestor-collapse).

title: 7.3 RESOLVE-COALESCING grill-me settled: three-outcome request memo + batch lookupAll (two-state entries, whole-batch outage)
rationale: Grill-me 2026-07-10 settled all Slice-7.3 forks; full design in docs/to-do/planning/RESOLVE-COALESCING/00-DESIGN.md. Keystones: (1) memo stores ALL THREE tri-state outcomes incl. the outage marker, pinning 'one request, one answer per target' as an ADR contract (revocation latency bounded by request duration; pass-through outside a web request); (2) batch resolve = lookupAll default method on RoleDefinitionSupplier — two-state entries, whole-batch outage, strict completeness (missing/extra entry = malformed = outage), GET wire on the same resolveCallGuard; (3) advice batching is UNCONDITIONAL code, the single flag opa.abac.resolve-memo.enabled governs memoization only (both role + ancestor memos — one knob one axis); (4) ancestor double-resolve fixed by a second memo decorator on the AncestorResolver bean (covers query path + advice via the starter's AncestorChainSupplier binding; both callers' distinct degrade semantics preserved); (5) merging the two list batch-evals REJECTED on layering (finisher at query time vs affordance at response time; verb sets live on web DTOs) — bound re-pinned to 2, not code-fixed; (6) memo-proof gap: multi-root pages (catalogs list) defeat duplicate-collapsing — batch seam is the fix; new k6 multi-root scenario lands EARLY on the branch so its baseline runs pre-memo. ADRs 0023 (memo) + 0024 (batch) up front at decompose.

description: A JWT->principal OncePerRequestFilter (AbacFilter) set the SecurityContext only when getAuthentication()==null. Installed via http.addFilterBefore(filter, AuthorizationFilter.class), it runs AFTER Spring Security's AnonymousAuthenticationFilter, which has already populated an AnonymousAuthenticationToken. So the guard saw a non-null auth, skipped, and every /api/** request was denied (403) by .authenticated().
resolution: Treat an AnonymousAuthenticationToken as 'not authenticated': attempt extraction when the current authentication is null OR an instanceof AnonymousAuthenticationToken; still never overwrite a real (non-anonymous) authentication. This lets the filter sit after AnonymousAuthenticationFilter and still take precedence.

title: Default JWT extractor requires explicit trust-forwarded-jwt opt-in
rationale: JwtClaimsSubjectExtractor verifies no signature by design (gateway-trust). Documented-but-unguarded meant a gateway-less deployment silently accepted self-minted tokens — total auth bypass. The starter now wires a refusing extractor (anonymous → deny + startup WARN) until opa.abac.subject.trust-forwarded-jwt=true; an app-supplied AbacSubjectExtractor bean bypasses the toggle. The dead verify-signature no-op property was removed (a security-named toggle that does nothing invites false safety). Rule: a dangerous default must be an explicit opt-in property, not a javadoc warning.

name: Gate-side resource resolution: split SPI + governing-root role + write-through request cache (ADR 0013 shape)
description: To make an annotation-driven pre-authorization gate decide on a resource's REAL attributes instead of a bare (type,id) reference: (1) one app-implemented AbacResourceResolver bean (Optional<AbacDataObject> resolve(type,id), dispatching internally) + a separate core AncestorChainSupplier the STARTER binds to the hierarchy resolver — the security module never sees data-module types; (2) the manager gains a constructor overload taking a ResourceResolutionSupport composition (resolver + nullable chainSupplier + cache); support absent => byte-identical baseline (pin with a serialized-context golden string test); (3) the role is resolved ONCE on the governing root (ancestors.isEmpty() ? leaf : ancestors.get(0)) so the gate decision equals the layer-3 decision it replaces; (4) split failure semantics, never confused: instance empty/throw -> DENY with no OPA call (an attribute-less context would WIDEN past attribute-keyed deny rules); ancestor throw -> collapse to empty chain, direct-only (never strips a direct grant); (5) the request-attributes cache is write-through on allow ONLY and never read by decisions — handlers reuse the authorized snapshot, decisions always resolve fresh; (6) a kill-switch property (default on, matchIfMissing) restores baseline semantics with beans untouched. Under an HTTP role source with exact target matching, the governing-root lookup is what closes the tag-blind realm-fallback hole on id'd member decisions.

name: B2 decomposition package: 5 tickets, the all-5-consumer sweep as the discipline
description: B2 (supplier-outage) decomposed into 5 tickets (docs/to-do/planning/B2-SUPPLIER-OUTAGE). Critical path T1 -> {T2,T3,T4} -> T5; T1+T2 the independently-landable subset (the library spine carrying the ONLY widening path). T1 core (RoleResolutionException + tri-state SPI javadoc, additive, Spring-free). T2 spring-security (the behavioral fix: explicit catch RoleResolutionException -> DENY in BOTH gate managers, before the existing broad catch-all; sibling test proves Optional.empty()->fallback unbroken). T3 spring-data (HierarchicalAuthorizer catch->false; SubtreeSpecResolver NO CODE CHANGE -> test-only proof its existing catch(RuntimeException) collapses the throw). T4 example (HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier strict classification: only 204->empty, only 200+valid->resolved, ALL else throws; CategoryListAuthorizer wrap->Page.empty; TeamRoleDefinitionSupplier catch DataAccessException->throw, conformant showcase; Demo javadoc). T5 e2e+headline IT (SupplierOutageGateIT: realm catalog-editor + supplier-throws -> 403 handler-never-ran; contrast 204->fallback grants) + whole-suite green (opa test 157/157 unchanged) + docs reconcile (PERMISSION-MODEL, ABAC-AUTHORIZATION). KEYSTONE DISCIPLINE baked into the decomposition + the prompt's hard rules + the ★ gate: this slice exists BECAUSE the PERMISSION-CATEGORIES review found 'the sweep stopped at the surface the ticket named' -> all 5 lookup() consumers are explicit tickets, a throw with no consumer test is an unfinished sweep. Pinned semantics in 01-DECOMPOSITION so the run never stops: outage->uniform 403 (no 503/kill-switch/error-code); strict 204-only HTTP invariant. Verify gate: PACKAGE OK. Ready for the autonomous run on feature/void3110/supplier-outage.

A Spring Boot starter registered its OPA-client JSON mapper as a top-level @Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean ObjectMapper. Because the application's primary ObjectMapper was now 'already defined' by the starter, Spring Boot's JacksonAutoConfiguration backed off — so the app's MVC message converter used a bare ObjectMapper with NO JSR-310 module, and every response/error carrying an OffsetDateTime (audit createdAt, ApiError.timestamp) failed to serialize: 'Java 8 date/time type not supported by default'. Manifested as 500s / wrong status codes deep in integration tests, far from the cause.
resolution: A library/starter must NEVER expose a primary ObjectMapper bean. Inject ObjectProvider<ObjectMapper> and use objectMapper.getIfAvailable(ObjectMapper::new): reuse the app's fully-configured mapper when present (keeping JSR-310 etc.), fall back to a private one only when absent. Same rule for any extractor/serializer that needs a mapper.

name: Ordered CMB fallback inside one auto-config: nested impl config + outer fallback bean method
description: When ONE auto-configuration must supply an opt-in impl (class+property gated) AND an always-present fail-closed default for the same interface, put the impl bean in a NESTED @Configuration (guarded by @ConditionalOnClass(name=...)+@ConditionalOnProperty) and the default as a @Bean method on the ENCLOSING class, both @ConditionalOnMissingBean(Interface.class). Member configurations register before the enclosing class's own bean methods, so the impl exists by the time the fallback's CMB evaluates — single-bean context in every state (off/on/adopter-override). Pin the ordering with an ApplicationContextRunner test asserting hasSingleBean + isInstanceOf on the ON state; if Spring ever changed member-first ordering the test fails loudly. Used by OpaDirectoryAutoConfiguration (UserDirectory: KeycloakUserDirectory vs NoOpUserDirectory, ADR 0020 §3); the optional module rides compileOnly on the starter like web/security/R4j.

name: Root-list membership isolation: drop the coarse :list gate, governed-scope IS the authority
description: Isolating a ROOT resource's list (catalog) by team membership, B4 T4. THE FORK (caught mid-T4, maintainer-approved): a :list endpoint is TYPE-LEVEL (@OpaPreAuthorize(catalog:list) has no resourceId), so OpaPreAuthorizeAuthorizationManager calls roleDefinitionSupplier.lookup(sub, type, NULL). Under the http (membership) profile HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier returns empty for a null resourceId -> no role_definition at the gate. Once T1 removed the realm fallback, catalog.allow for :list with no role-def DENIES -> the coarse gate would deny EVERY membership-driven caller. (Latent: all existing matrices run under the DEMO profile, where DemoRoleDefinitionSupplier ignores resourceId and resolves a role at type-level, so the gate passed there.) RESOLUTION: DROP the @OpaPreAuthorize(catalog:list) annotation entirely; CatalogListAuthorizer is the SOLE authority via findAuthorized(catalogs, governedScope, ctx, null, pageable). The governed-scope (id IN governed-ids, else denyAll) AND filter-residual cut is fail-closed to empty, so it subsumes 'may you list at all' (governs nothing -> []). Contrast CATEGORY list: category is NOT a root — category:list passes the coarse gate via list_inheritable_grant (the role resolved on the catalogId parent), and CategoryListAuthorizer scopes by catalogId. A root has no parent to resolve on. WHICH ROLE drives the role-def-only filter residual for a root list: resolve on the FIRST governed id (governedIds.get(0)) — any governed catalog's membership role answers the coarse 'may I list'; the per-row cut is the governed scope. SPI SHAPE: GovernedScopeResolver exposes governedIds(subject,type):List<UUID> as the primitive + a DEFAULT governedScope built from it, so ONE membership fetch drives both the scope and the role lookup (the first draft probed catalogs.findAll() per-id = table scan + N HTTP calls = rejected at review). findAuthorized composes scope.and(residual).and(notDenied), so governedScope(base) ∧ ALLOW_ALL = governed set, ∧ DENY_ALL = empty. IT technique: a TestGovernedScopeResolver (per-subject ids) + a @Primary ProgrammableOpaClient (compile->allowAll/denyAll) + catalog.role-source=none (disables DemoRoleDefinitionSupplier) proves the SQL row-cut against real Postgres without live OPA. GOTCHA: PaginationEnvelopeIT asserted catalog count>=1; post-B4 the permissive IT wires no resolver -> count 0, relaxed to >=0 (envelope contract holds; row-cut proven in CatalogListIsolationIT). No e2e matrix asserts a catalog-list count (all status-only) so E8 unaffected.

name: 5-consumer sweep for a RoleDefinitionSupplier SPI change: gate x2 + hierarchy + subtree + list
description: An SPI-contract change to RoleDefinitionSupplier.lookup() must sweep ALL FIVE production consumers, not just the one the ticket names (the review lesson 'the sweep stopped at the surface the ticket named', PERMISSION-CATEGORIES-REVIEW). The five, with their B2 outage mapping: (1) OpaPreAuthorizeAuthorizationManager -> explicit catch(RoleResolutionException) -> DENY before the broad catch(Exception); (2) OpaAuthorizationManager -> same; both are the ONLY consumers with a realm fallback, so they carry the only widening path — the outage must deny BEFORE any OpaClient call so the fallback is never fed an outage input (assert verify(opaClient, never()).allow). (3) HierarchicalAuthorizer -> catch around the governing-root lookup -> return false (no fallback in this seam; needed a new catch + a logger field, the throw previously ESCAPED uncaught). (4) SubtreeSpecResolver -> NO CODE CHANGE (its existing catch(RuntimeException)->Optional.empty() already collapses it) but ADD a test pinning the SPECIFIC RoleResolutionException type so a refactor can't silently widen. (5) CategoryListAuthorizer (example) -> catch -> Page.empty(pageable) (the direct lookup escaped -> would be a 500; the SubtreeSpecResolver path it also calls is already fail-closed). Plus 4 implementors: NoOp/Demo never throw (in-process -> additivity), Http classifies (the fix), Team* minimal touch (DataAccessException->throw). A throw with NO consumer test = an unfinished sweep.

name: Fault-injecting e2e: a stdlib resolve stub, two passes over one rig, proving transient-recovers vs sustained-denies (B3 T4)
description: Proving a resilience headline through the gateway needs a FAULT INJECTOR the existing newman harness lacks. The smallest one: a stdlib python http.server stub (infra/resilience-stub/resolve_stub.py) standing in for the resolve endpoint, run on python:3.12-alpine with the script MOUNTED (no image build). STUB_MODE=transient returns N (STUB_FAILS) 503s PER CALLER KEY then the role; STUB_MODE=down returns 503 always. deploy.sh ENABLE_RESILIENCE_STUB=1 points the catalog role-source=http at resolve-stub:8080 INSTEAD of the real user-mgmt (a separate elif before ENABLE_USER_SERVICE), and starts/stops the stub in the up/down lifecycle. The matrix asserts the CUT in TWO PASSES OVER ONE RIG: the runner docker-compose force-recreates the stub in each mode between passes (resetting the per-key counters), so a single stand-up proves E1 (transient -> 200) and E2 (down -> 403). The collection reads EXPECTED_STATUS per pass and, for the 403 pass, ALSO asserts not within(200,299) — so a regression letting a sustained outage ride the realm fallback to a 2xx FAILS the matrix. LIVE-RUN GOTCHAS that bit and are now fixed: (1) the protected route is /api/v1/catalogs/{catalogId}/categories/{categoryId} (NESTED under catalogs), NOT a flat /categories/{id} — a flat URL 404s (handler not-found), not 403, so the gate-passed-but-wrong-url symptom looks like a resolve failure but isn't. (2) the psql fixture seed needs the NOT-NULL created_at + tags ('{}'::jsonb) columns AND the ltree path (text2ltree('catalog_'||hex) for the catalog, '...category_'||hex appended for the category) — the naive (id,name,version) insert fails on created_at. (3) mint the token IN-NETWORK (docker run --network ...curl against keycloak:8888) — APISIX validates the issuer, a localhost:28888 token is rejected. (4) the rig needs ./profile.sh up (base Postgres) BEFORE deploy.sh up, else deploy.sh exits 'Postgres not running'. Zero Rego this slice -> no OPA restart, opa test 183/183 unchanged. Pinned by ADR 0017; the headline is P9. Relates to mx-24ac37 (the resolve wrapper this e2e exercises).

A circuit breaker wrapping a fail-closed authorization call must NOT count a returned fail-closed SENTINEL as a breaker failure — only a THROWN fault. B3's Resilience4jCallGuard.call recorded breaker.onError() on BOTH the retryable-exception path AND the retryable-RESULT path. The OPA decorator retries on the returned sentinel (allow=false / compile fromError / all-false), which is INDISTINGUISHABLE from a genuine policy DENY. So every legitimate deny recorded a breaker failure on the long-lived shared OPA breaker; with maxRetries=1 (2 attempts/request) + failureThreshold=5, ~3 consecutive deny requests SELF-OPEN the breaker, after which every OPA call (incl. ones that would be ALLOWED) fails closed for the open window (10s). NOT a fail-open (outcome stays fail-closed — denies MORE), but a self-inflicted availability regression that violates the breaker's own invariant 'never a decision input' (ADR 0017 section 5). The run's own ★ gate + green tests MISSED it because the only breaker-open test opened the breaker via the deny sentinel itself (masking the bug); the multi-lens adversarial completeness critic caught it.
resolution: Record a breaker failure ONLY on the thrown retryableError path (an unambiguous transport/timeout fault), never on a returned retryable sentinel. A returned sentinel is still RETRIED (transient recovery preserved) but never feeds the breaker. Consequence (honest, document it): the resolve/tag breakers still open (those edges surface a real outage as a THROWN Transient*Exception → the exception path), while the OPA breaker becomes effectively a no-op (HttpOpaClient swallows every fault into the sentinel and never throws) — the correct price of a swallow-everything delegate, strictly better than decision-driven self-opening. GENERAL RULE: when a resilience wrapper sits over a fail-closed call that returns its failure as a VALUE rather than throwing, the breaker can only be driven by exceptions; a breaker that opens on the fail-closed value conflates 'the dependency is down' with 'the policy said no'. Add a test asserting N>threshold consecutive genuine denials keep the breaker CLOSED. Pinned by docs/code-review/B3-HTTP-RESILIENCE-REVIEW.md (M1/L1).

name: Additive evolution of a public Jackson-serialized record (byte-for-byte back-compat)
description: To add fields to a published, OPA-input-serialized record (core.RoleDefinition) without breaking the wire or any caller: (1) add optional record components annotated @JsonProperty(snake_case) @JsonInclude(NON_EMPTY/NON_NULL) so when unused they are ABSENT and an old role serializes byte-for-byte as before; (2) normalize dependent fields to null when the feature is off — match_mode is null unless required_tags is non-empty, else defaults to ANY_OF — so the absent-field invariant holds and the stored row agrees with the resolved object; (3) keep the prior-arity constructor as a convenience delegate (new 3-arg -> 5-arg with empty/null) so every existing caller compiles unchanged; (4) Jackson fills missing record components with null on deserialize, which the compact constructor normalizes, so old payloads still parse. PROVE additivity with a whole-repo ./gradlew build (every old test unchanged) PLUS a byte-shape assertion (the serialized JSON has EXACTLY the old field names). This was the single allowed library change for the whole tag-dictionary slice; the other library modules stayed untouched (git diff --name-only).

name: Commit-time constraint violations dodge the 409 advice: flush inside the @Transactional method
description: A DataIntegrityViolationException raised at TRANSACTION COMMIT (the default flush point) surfaces from the @Transactional proxy as an untranslated wrapper (e.g. TransactionSystemException) that a @RestControllerAdvice @ExceptionHandler(DataIntegrityViolationException) never catches -> the FK conflict answers 500 even though the advice exists. The deterministic fix: repository.flush() INSIDE the transactional service method right after the violating write (e.g. roles.delete(role); roles.flush()), so Spring's exception translation runs in-method and the typed exception propagates to the advice -> 409 STATE_CONFLICT. Found wiring the in-use-role-delete 409 (retro-audit follow-up); the 5.97 starter advice alone was NOT sufficient without the in-method flush. Pinned by ErrorContractIT.deletingAnInUseCustomRoleIsProblemJsonWithStateConflict.

content: A security starter must NOT register its own SecurityFilterChain — it exposes beans and the application owns the chain. The opa-abac starter wires OpaClient/RoleDefinitionSupplier/AbacSubjectExtractor/AbacFilter/@OpaPreAuthorize-advisor as @ConditionalOnMissingBean, with the security beans additionally @ConditionalOnClass({SecurityFilterChain, OncePerRequestFilter}) (string-name form, isolated in an imported config so the types never load in a non-web app). The application declares @EnableWebSecurity @EnableMethodSecurity, builds its own SecurityFilterChain, and installs the injected AbacFilter (.addFilterBefore(abacFilter, AuthorizationFilter.class)). Inject AbacFilter via ObjectProvider so a permissive test profile (opa.abac.enabled=false) without the filter still builds a chain. Also disable Boot's auto-registration of the filter as a top-level servlet filter (a disabled FilterRegistrationBean) so it runs ONLY inside the security chain. Asserted in ApplicationContextRunner: doesNotHaveBean(SecurityFilterChain) when the starter is on.

name: Tri-state RoleDefinitionSupplier: outage throws, no-role is empty, each consumer maps to its own fail-closed
description: B2 closes the one widening-on-failure path: RoleDefinitionSupplier.lookup() became TRI-STATE so a role-source OUTAGE can't be mistaken for an authoritative NO-ROLE. Optional.of=resolved; Optional.empty()=authoritative no-role (a DESIGNED signal — the policy may fall back to realm roles, RETAINED); throw RoleResolutionException=outage (source unavailable, result UNKNOWN -> caller MUST fail closed, never fall back). RoleResolutionException is a new unchecked RuntimeException in opa-abac-core (Spring-free; mirrors AncestorResolutionException but a SEPARATE failure axis — never conflate role-source-outage with ancestor-chain-collapse). Mechanism: the SUPPLIER classifies (throws on outage) — the one place classification lives — and EACH consumer CATCHES and maps the throw to its OWN fail-closed outcome. NO library wrapper: a wrapper that caught->empty would re-introduce the exact bug, and 'deny' is not uniform across consumers (403 at a gate vs empty-page vs no-subtree-widening). The safety discipline is the explicit contract + a mandatory per-consumer outage test cell, not a runtime transform. Pinned in ADR 0014.

name: CallGuard: a backend-agnostic resilience seam that retries on result AND exception, with an injectable clock
description: Slice B3's cross-service HTTP resilience is built on a thin CallGuard seam (in opa-abac-spring-security, package …security.resilience) so opa-abac-core stays Spring-free and the Boot-4/Spring-7 native-resilience backend is a later ONE-IMPL swap, not a three-edge rewrite. Three non-obvious shape decisions: (1) call(Supplier<T> body, Predicate<Throwable> retryableError, Predicate<T> retryableResult) takes TWO predicates — the edges classify an HTTP failure AFTER a successful send() (a 5xx comes back as a normal HttpResponse, only a transport fault throws), and the OPA decorator's delegate NEVER throws (HttpOpaClient catches everything internally), so a retry-on-exception-only guard could never retry either. The result predicate is mandatory, not optional. (2) On exhaustion the guard re-throws the LAST CAUSE UNCHANGED (asserted isSameAs) / returns the last value unchanged — the caller's fail-closed mapping (T3's B2 RoleResolutionException, the OPA decorator's PartialResult.error()) depends on seeing the original outcome, never an R4j RetryException wrapper. Breaker-open throws a backend-agnostic CallNotPermittedException (NOT R4j's), so the backend can swap without changing any caller's catch. (3) DETERMINISTIC TIMING is a design constraint on the seam, not a test afterthought: inject BOTH a java.time.Clock (drives the breaker's open-duration window) AND a sleeper (LongConsumer<millis>) the tests stub to advance a MutableClock — so full-jitter exponential backoff is real in prod yet instant+observable in tests (assert bounds ≤ ceiling, never exact waits); zero Thread.sleep, zero wall-clock. R4j GOTCHA: CircuitBreaker.of(name,cfg) has NO clock overload in R4j 2.x — the only public seam to inject a Clock is new io.github.resilience4j.circuitbreaker.internal.CircuitBreakerStateMachine(name, cfg, clock); isolate that one internal-package line in a buildBreaker() helper. Breaker is failure-COUNT based (failureRateThreshold=100% over a count window sized to failureThreshold), not latency based — so the recorded call duration is irrelevant (report 0), matching ADR 0017 §5 'the breaker is a load optimization, never a decision input'. Asymmetric per-edge budgets via a ResilienceConfig record (enabled/maxRetries/backoff/ceiling/failureThreshold/openDuration/halfOpenProbes); enabled=false → a single unguarded attempt, byte-identical to pre-B3. Pinned by ADR 0017; T1 of B3.

name: Keycloak-admin directory client: timeout-bounded jakarta Client + cause-chain 401 classification
description: Wrapping org.keycloak:keycloak-admin-client (26.x) as a fail-closed read seam needs two non-obvious moves. (1) The default admin client has NO timeouts — pass KeycloakBuilder.resteasyClient(ClientBuilder.newBuilder().connectTimeout/readTimeout(...)...build()); RESTEasy provider auto-discovery makes the bare jakarta.ws.rs ClientBuilder work with no explicit Jackson registration. (2) The client WRAPS the token grant's 401 — the exception surfacing to the caller is a wrapper whose CAUSE is jakarta.ws.rs.NotAuthorizedException, so a typed catch misclassifies grant failures; classify by walking getCause() (isAuthFailure) to keep the distinct WARN-per-edge contract. Also: client construction does no I/O (token is lazy) so a down IdP surfaces in search() as the no-oracle empty, never at startup; re-enforce the result-size clamp with .limit(clamped) because a misbehaving server may ignore max.

name: Read-side affordance enrichment: ResponseBodyAdvice + Enrichable marker + per-type sub-interface registry + x-implements codegen + allowAll refold
description: Action enrichment ships a read-side _actions affordance map via a ResponseBodyAdvice, with a low-ceremony per-type opt-in that doubles as the registry. THE PATTERN: (1) a library marker interface Enrichable (opa-abac-spring-security ...security.web) declaring getId/getActions/setActions PLUS abstract abacResourceType()/abacActions() — the advice reads the latter two off an Enrichable reference, so they must be on the BASE, not only the sub-interface. (2) An app per-type sub-interface (CategoryEnrichable extends Enrichable) supplies abacResourceType()+abacActions() as DEFAULTS — this sub-interface IS the action registry AND the validation allowlist; no SPI bean, no runtime class->type map. (3) OpenAPI x-implements: [<sub-interface FQN>] on the schema makes the spring generator emit `implements <sub-interface>`; a property named _actions becomes getActions()/setActions() (JavaBeans strips the leading underscore) with @JsonProperty("_actions") + Map<String,Boolean> — matching Enrichable exactly, NO generator config. (4) The advice groups returned DTOs by type, reads each resolved snapshot from the request-scoped AbacResourceCache (5.97; the list path write-throughs survivors so single+list share one read path), resolves the governing-root role (ancestors.isEmpty()?leaf:ancestors[0], mirroring HierarchicalAuthorizer), builds the flat rows x verbs context list (row-major i*V+j), calls OpaClient.allowAll ONCE per type (the Phase-5 bulk primitive, reused verbatim), and re-folds the positional booleans into per-row bare-verb maps. Adoption per type = one sub-interface (2 default methods) + two schema lines. Kill-switch opa.abac.action-enrichment.enabled; starter gates the advice on @ConditionalOnBean(AbacResourceResolver)+AllNestedConditions(resource-resolution.enabled && action-enrichment.enabled) — the exact conditions producing the cache it reads.

A custom AuthorizationManager<MethodInvocation> for a method annotation (e.g. @OpaPreAuthorize) read the annotation off invocation.getMethod(), which on a proxied bean is the INTERFACE method — so the method-level annotation on the concrete impl was never found and the manager abstained (returned null), silently letting every call through. Also a bare @EnableMethodSecurity context did not apply a hand-declared AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor @Bean to the target proxy, so the slice test never intercepted at all.
resolution: In the manager, resolve the most-specific method before reading the annotation: AopUtils.getMostSpecificMethod(invocation.getMethod(), targetClass) where targetClass = invocation.getThis().getClass(); read the annotation (and discover SpEL parameter names) off THAT method, falling back to the class-level annotation. In tests, drive the real AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor via ProxyFactory.addAdvisor(interceptor) (NOT addAdvice, which discards the interceptor's own @OpaPreAuthorize pointcut) so its pointcut gates the proxied method; allow runs, deny throws AccessDeniedException.

title: 7.3 deep review: approved with fixes (1 Low); the run's own review gates held under an 8-lens adversarial pass
rationale: The RESOLVE-COALESCING deep review (Path 2B: 8 failure-mode lenses -> adversarial refutation -> completeness critic, 11 agents) confirmed ZERO Critical/Medium on a 51-file autonomous-run branch; the single Low was a stale runner-header comment (the action-enrichment runner's E-cell descriptions predated ADR 0022 and the 7.3 E7 cells) — fixed in-review. Notable: the per-ticket architecture-review gates during the run had already caught and fixed the two defects an ordinary post-hoc review would have headlined (the advisor eager-injection decorator bypass; the allowAll any-false retry), which is the flow working as designed — the post-run review's residual finding rate collapses when the in-run gate is real. Review note: docs/code-review/RESOLVE-COALESCING-REVIEW.md.

name: Resilient OpaClient: a BeanPostProcessor decorator + retry-on-fail-closed-sentinel (B3 T2)
description: B3's OPA-edge resilience is a ResilientOpaClient that wraps the plain OpaClient through the OPA CallGuard, auto-configured by the starter @ConditionalOnClass(io.github.resilience4j.circuitbreaker.CircuitBreaker) + an AllNestedConditions over resilience.enabled + resilience.opa.enabled (both matchIfMissing=true). TWO non-obvious mechanics: (1) WIRING via a BeanPostProcessor, NOT a second @Bean OpaClient. The plain opaClient bean is @ConditionalOnMissingBean and a user override must keep winning; a BPP's postProcessAfterInitialization decorates WHATEVER OpaClient the context ended up with (starter HttpOpaClient OR an adopter bean) without competing for the bean name — the wrapper is transparent to every injection point. Build the CallGuard LAZILY inside the BPP (volatile + null-check) from an ObjectProvider<OpaAbacProperties>, because a BPP is instantiated BEFORE @ConfigurationProperties binding completes — deferring guard construction to first-wrap (which runs at OpaClient init, well after binding) is what makes the bound budgets visible. GOTCHA: this wraps a USER-supplied OpaClient too (correct — resilience applies to any client), which breaks any existing test asserting the bean is directly the user's stub type; fix that test by running it with resilience.enabled=false and add a separate wrap-the-user-bean test (build-breaker lands in the same commit). (2) RETRY-ON-FAIL-CLOSED-SENTINEL. HttpOpaClient swallows every transport/parse failure into its fail-closed value and NEVER throws, so the decorator cannot retry on an exception — it retries on the RETURNED sentinel: compile on PartialResult.fromError() (the EXACT failure flag, cleanly distinct from a real denyAll() whose fromError=false), allow on the false result, allowAll when any element is false. A genuine policy deny ALSO retries — accepted because the OPA gate is a local sidecar at 1 retry/~50ms and an OPA decision is deterministic (a real deny stays false, never widens): one extra fast hop on a deny, fail-closed fully intact, while a transient blip recovers the real answer (the B3 headline). The decorator OWNS the fail-closed values on breaker-open (CallNotPermittedException → the delegate was never called): false / PartialResult.error() (fromError=true, NEVER denyAll()/allowAll() — a denyAll() lets a 5.5-B hierarchy subtreeSpec widening survive an OPA outage) / n×false. Config: OpaAbacProperties.Resilience{enabled, Edge opa/resolve/tag}, Edge.toConfig(masterEnabled) folds master+edge switches into the ResilienceConfig record. R4j is an OPTIONAL starter dep — it arrives transitively as api from opa-abac-spring-security; U8 proves both classpath states via FilteredClassLoader(CircuitBreaker.class). Pinned by ADR 0017 §1/§2/§6.

name: Strict HTTP role-source classification: only 204->empty, only 200+valid->resolved, everything else throws
description: The B2 HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier classification invariant (ADR 0014 section 4): stop swallowing failures. ONLY 204 -> Optional.empty() (authoritative no-role -> the policy realm fallback may decide). ONLY 200+non-blank+parseable body -> Optional.of(resolved). EVERYTHING ELSE THROWS RoleResolutionException (outage -> deny): 200-blank (a contract-violating 200 is untrustworthy, not no-role), ALL 4xx (the resolve protocol is not working as designed — never the designed 204), ALL 5xx, timeout, connection-refused/IOException, malformed-200 (Jackson parse failure). Treating any non-204 as no-role lets a misrouted/misconfigured/corrupt response silently WIDEN via the realm fallback — the whole bug. Impl notes: use NARROW catches (IOException / InterruptedException / JacksonException), NOT a broad catch(Exception), so a programming bug (e.g. NPE) is not mislabeled as an outage; restore the interrupt flag on InterruptedException before throwing; WARN with status-code or exception-class ONLY — never the userId/token/body (assert this with a no-PII test). Resilience (retry/backoff) is a SEPARATE axis -> Slice B3, not here.

Action enrichment's omit-on-failure contract collides with OpaClient.allowAll's fail-closed-to-all-false. HttpOpaClient.allowAll NEVER throws and NEVER returns a short list — on any error (non-200, timeout, malformed, mixed-type) it returns a FULL-LENGTH all-false list. So a ResponseBodyAdvice consuming allowAll cannot distinguish a transport failure from a genuine all-deny by the returned booleans alone, and a decomposition that assumes 'allowAll throws or shortens on failure' (as the enrichment T2 acceptance did) would silently emit a fabricated all-false _actions map on an OPA outage — the exact fail-open-looking-like-fail-closed footgun ADR 0016 §7 forbids.
resolution: Treat an all-false verb block as could-not-compute -> OMIT the row's _actions (settled with the maintainer). Zero OpaClient change, no extra round-trip, strictly fail-closed (can never fabricate). Cost: a genuinely fully-denied resource loses its honest all-false map, but that is rare since a caller reaching enrichment already passed a gated read (view is normally true). The advice ALSO omits on a throwing custom client and a short/mismatched list, so the contract holds for any OpaClient impl. KEY LESSON for future read-side allowAll consumers: allowAll's all-false IS the filtering consumer's correct degrade (drop the row), but it is the WRONG degrade for any consumer that must distinguish deny from could-not-compute — they must treat all-false as ambiguous.

title: 5.97 decomposition pinned two contract semantics the design left implicit (missing-id 403; conjunct over scope-out)
rationale: Decomposing RESOURCE-RESOLUTION surfaced two externally-visible semantics ADR 0013 implied but never stated, and pinned them in 01-DECOMPOSITION so the autonomous run never stops to ask: (1) ADR 0013's 'resolver empty/throws -> DENY' read literally means a MISSING id behind an annotated resourceId answers 403 where it answered 404 pre-5.97 (the gate denies before the handler can 404); wrong-scope-but-existing stays the handler's 404. Consequence found at decompose time: the catalog CRUD ITs must run with opa.abac.resource-resolution.enabled=false (they test CRUD, not authz) and double as the kill-switch off-state proof, while a new ResourceResolutionGateIT owns the gate cells - otherwise every missing-id IT/e2e cell flips red mid-run. (2) The retro-audit fold-in offered 'tags_satisfied conjunct OR documented category-only scope' for product/catalog.rego; the package picks the conjunct (mirror category.rego verbatim, vacuous back-compat) per the audit's security-first disposition. Both flagged for maintainer review of the package. The general lesson: a fail-closed rule at the GATE re-types not-found from 404 to 403 on every annotated id'd endpoint - any slice that moves a decision earlier in the request lifecycle must sweep the status-code contract of the paths it now preempts.

title: Fail-closed has two shapes: empty-for-deny (role/decision) vs reject (validation-input fetch)
rationale: A role/decision supplier (HttpRoleDefinitionSupplier) fails closed to Optional.empty(): the policy then default-denies — empty is the safe value. But a fetch whose result is a VALIDATION INPUT (the tag dictionary the catalog validates assigned tags against) must fail closed to a REJECTION, not an empty set: an empty applicable-set would make every tag illegal-by-absence or, worse, be misread as all-allowed — either way it WIDENS or corrupts legality. So TagDefinitionClient throws TagDefinitionFetchException on any non-200/timeout/refused/malformed; the catalog turns that into 503 and persists nothing. Rule of thumb: when the fetched value GATES a decision, empty=deny is fail-closed; when it CONSTRAINS what is legal, empty is unsafe — reject instead. Validation across the two example apps is by the wire CONTRACT (TagDefinitionView), not a shared class — a shared validator would force a non-additive library change.

description: A 'zero Rego change' / 'the primitive already exists for every type' invariant in a slice's design can be FALSE for types that never exercised it. Phase 6 action enrichment assumed the per-type OPA bulk rule existed for every enriched type; it existed ONLY in category.rego (the one type whose LIST used the Phase-5 allowlist-batch path that consumes bulk). catalog/product/team had NO bulk rule, so enriching them made OpaClient.allowAll read an empty OPA result -> the client fail-closes to all-false -> the advice all-false-means-omit -> _actions silently absent. Only Category enriched live. CRITICAL: invisible to every unit+IT test because they stub allowAll / use a programmable OpaClient and never hit the real OPA bulk rule absence — it surfaced ONLY in the live e2e through the gateway against real OPA. Second bug same ticket: the OpenAPI-generated DTO inits the _actions Map field to an empty HashMap, so an UNSET map serializes as {} on the wire (not absent); a client reads {} as a fabricated all-deny, violating omit-never-fabricate. Also invisible to object-level assertions (a round-tripped DTO reads back {} regardless) — only a raw-JSON/wire assertion catches it.
resolution: (1) bulk gap: add the identical decision-preserving bulk entrypoint (allow mapped over input.items via a comprehension) to every enriched type's rego, mirroring the one type that has it byte-for-byte, + mirrored opa-test cases; reframe the invariant as 'zero change to existing decision logic; the batch primitive is EXTENDED to the newly-consuming types'. (2) empty-map: put @JsonInclude(NON_EMPTY) on the LIBRARY marker getter (Enrichable.getActions) — Jackson honors an interface-declared annotation on the implementing generated getter, so every adopter omits the empty/unset map for free. GENERAL LESSONS for any 'reuse an existing primitive across new consumers' slice: (a) VERIFY the primitive exists for EVERY new consumer, not just the one that introduced it (grep per type, do not assume); (b) a 'reuses X verbatim, zero change' claim must be checked against EACH new call site in PLANNING; (c) a contract whose correctness lives in the SERIALIZED form (absent vs {} vs null) needs a WIRE-level e2e assertion — object-level unit/IT cannot see it; (d) the live e2e is the only layer that exercises the real policy engine + the real serializer, not optional polish.

description: REFINED auto-config gating for a starter advice that depends on a conditionally-produced bean (extends the earlier @ConditionalOnBean-ordering record). Phase 6 enrichment's ActionEnrichmentAdvice needs the AbacResourceCache bean, which ResourceResolutionAutoConfiguration produces ONLY under {a resolver @Component bean AND resource-resolution.enabled}. Two wrong gates were tried and both broke: (1) @ConditionalOnBean(AbacResourceCache.class) — order-unreliable even when the cache is declared in an EARLIER sibling nested @Configuration of the SAME @AutoConfiguration (the ApplicationContextRunner U11 test failed: the advice config is evaluated before the sibling's cache bean registers). (2) @ConditionalOnBean(AbacResourceResolver.class) alone — passes U11, but the catalog ships a CatalogResourceResolver @Component that is ALWAYS present, so the advice activated even in the resolution-OFF IT suites (which boot resource-resolution.enabled=false), where NO cache bean exists -> context-startup NoSuchBeanDefinitionException broke 33 ITs. The failure only surfaced on the FULL ./gradlew build (the example ITs), never in the starter's own ApplicationContextRunner tests.
resolution: Gate on @ConditionalOnBean(AbacResourceResolver.class) (reliable: the resolver is a user/@Component-supplied bean) PLUS an AllNestedConditions that ANDs BOTH @ConditionalOnProperty(resource-resolution.enabled) and @ConditionalOnProperty(action-enrichment.enabled), both matchIfMissing=true — i.e. mirror EXACTLY the conditions under which the depended-on bean is produced. (@ConditionalOnProperty is not @Repeatable, so the two property checks must be combined via an AllNestedConditions subclass referenced by @Conditional(Outer.Inner.class) with the fully-qualified nested name.) GENERAL RULES: (a) when an auto-config bean has a hard dependency on another conditionally-produced bean, gate it on the SAME conditions that produce the dependency, not on a proxy like the resolver bean (resolver-present != cache-produced when a kill-switch is off). (b) @ConditionalOnBean is reliable only against user/@Component beans, NEVER against sibling auto-config beans, even in declaration order. (c) Such mis-gating is invisible to ApplicationContextRunner unit tests that always supply the dependency — only the FULL build (the real app ITs, esp. kill-switch-off profiles) catches it; always run ./gradlew build before declaring an auto-config ticket done. SEPARATELY: a resolution-ON gate IT that asserts an exact role-lookup/OPA-call COUNT must disable action-enrichment (it adds its own governing-root role lookup per enriched row) — turn enrichment off in gate-focused suites; enrichment gets its own ITs.

description: Two rig/probe gotchas that made the 7.4 security-review live-probe phase yield probed:0 and nearly produced a false refutation of a real finding. (1) The rig OPA container at localhost:8181 was loaded with an UNRELATED policy bundle (a paas/projects corpus), NOT this repo catalog/category/product policies, so every data.catalog.* HTTP query returned only a decision_id with no result field (undefined doc). Any live authz probe against that OPA silently proves nothing. Check GET /v1/policies (or GET /v1/data top keys) FIRST to confirm the repo bundle is mounted before trusting a live-rig authz probe. (2) opa eval with the -i flag treats the ENTIRE file as input, so an input JSON wrapped as an object with a top-level input key makes OPA see input.input.* and the real fields resolve to empty — every rule fails for an unrelated reason (a spurious false). ALSO catalog.rego computes verb by splitting input.action on the colon, so the action must be catalog:view not view, or verb is undefined. An early mis-shaped probe returned false on a genuinely-true (buggy) allow, caught only by adding a no-deny baseline case that ALSO returned false, exposing the input as broken rather than the policy as safe.
resolution: PROBE HYGIENE for OPA findings: (a) confirm the correct bundle is loaded (GET /v1/policies) before any live-rig authz probe, else fall back to opa eval -d infra/opa/policies against the repo files (authoritative for static-policy defects). (b) opa eval with -i wants the BARE input object (strip any top-level input wrapper). (c) action strings need the type prefix like catalog:view. (d) ALWAYS run a positive baseline (same input minus the deny/negative condition): if the baseline that should ALLOW returns false, the probe is mis-shaped, not the policy safe. Same assert-the-cut-not-the-shape discipline, applied to the probe itself.

title: Multi-root list resolve bound re-pinned to 2: the query-time coarse role + the response-time batch are two questions at two lifecycle points
rationale: 7.3 T5 discovered during the review gate that the design's 'multi-root resolve M -> 1' acceptance was unreachable WITHOUT widening: CatalogListAuthorizer resolves the caller's role on the FIRST governed id at QUERY time (the coarse role driving the filter residual — fail-closed load-bearing; a role explicitly denying list must compile DENY_ALL, so the resolve cannot be removed), while the enrichment batch runs at RESPONSE time over the page's distinct roots. The memo dedups the shared root (the batch excludes it as a hit) but the two exchanges cannot merge — the exact 'two questions, two lifecycle points' shape that re-pinned the list's batch-eval bound from 1 to 2 (finisher vs affordance). Post-7.3 multi-root wire shape: 1 single + 1 lookupAll = 2 resolve calls (was M+1 = 51 measured); same-root scenarios stay at 1 because every caller shares one key, the memo collapses them, and a fully-hit batch never delegates. Pinned in amplification.py EXPECTED with rationale; the PERFORMANCE.md 7.3 ledger carries 51 -> 2. Lesson for planning: an acceptance bound spanning MULTIPLE lifecycle points should be derived per call-site (query-time vs response-time), not per page.

description: The example services' OpenAPI ProblemDetail.errorCode is a CLOSED enum ('the union of codes this service can emit'). When the starter's PersistenceConflictProblemAdvice started emitting STATE_CONFLICT (5.97), neither catalog-api.yaml nor user-mgmt-api.yaml gained the value -- the catalog under-documented its I4/I5 409s for a whole slice, and the audit-followups branch made the same code reachable in user-mgmt (in-use-role-delete) without touching the spec. A generated client deserializing into the closed enum fails on the undeclared value. Found by the deep-review api-contract lens; the catalog mirror only by the completeness critic (a per-file lens is structurally blind to the sibling spec).
resolution: Both enums extended with STATE_CONFLICT (audit-followups-hardening branch). Rule: whenever a starter advice or handler starts emitting a LibraryErrorCode on a service's wire, grep BOTH specs' errorCode enums in the same commit -- the enum is part of the error contract, and 'reachable but undeclared' survives green builds because nothing validates emitted codes against the spec.

description: ToolRegistry (example-mcp-server T1) documented 'declaration order' for all()/names() but returned List.copyOf(byName.values()) over a Map.copyOf map. Map.copyOf gives NO iteration-order guarantee and randomizes order PER JVM RUN (immutable-collection SALT), so the advertised tool order was nondeterministic across restarts and the javadoc contract was false. Caught only because a later ticket's test run drew a different order and a containsExactly assertion failed - a single green run proves nothing about this class of bug. It was not cosmetic: the roster pre-flight (T5) sends one AbacContext per registered tool through OpaClient.allowAll and matches the returned booleans BY INDEX against the tool list, so an unstable order is precisely the index-shift the roster's acceptance case forbids - a tool could be advertised as allowed on the strength of a different tool's decision.
resolution: Keep an immutable declaration-ordered List<ToolDescriptor> alongside the lookup map (List.copyOf over LinkedHashMap.values(), which IS insertion-ordered); serve all() from it and derive names() from it so the two are positionally aligned by construction. Regression test asserts index-for-index alignment and repeat-read stability. GENERAL RULE for this repo: any collection whose ORDER is part of a contract - especially one paired positionally with a batch OPA response - must be held as a List, never read back out of a Map.copyOf/Set.copyOf. Reach for Map.copyOf only for pure key lookup.

title: Gate MCP tool calls by wrapping the SyncToolSpecification callHandler, not with a Spring AOP aspect
rationale: Decided during AGENT-TOOL-AUTHZ T4 (2026-07-28). Spring AI 2.0.0 auto-configuration produces a List<McpServerFeatures.SyncToolSpecification> bean (bean name toolSpecs) from the @McpTool annotation scanner; each spec is a record of (McpSchema.Tool, BiFunction<McpSyncServerExchange, CallToolRequest, CallToolResult> callHandler). Wrapping that callHandler via a BeanPostProcessor over the list is the interception point, for three reasons. (1) UNBYPASSABLE: the handler IS what the MCP server invokes for tools/call, so nothing routes around it - whereas a Spring AOP aspect on the @McpTool method only fires for calls through the beans proxy, and the annotation scanner builds callbacks from the bean instance it was handed, so whether the aspect sits in the invocation path depends on proxy-unwrapping behaviour we do not control and that can change in a minor upgrade. For a gate whose whole purpose is to be the one an untrusted host cannot skip, probably-in-the-path is not a gate. (2) NO ENUMERATION: post-processing wraps whatever the scanner found, so a tool added later cannot be forgotten. (3) NO NEW DEPENDENCY: no spring-boot-starter-aop. GOTCHA the wiring test found: the context holds MORE THAN ONE List<SyncToolSpecification> bean - toolSpecs (populated, from the annotation scanner) and syncTools (EMPTY, for ToolCallback-style tools). Injecting List<SyncToolSpecification> by type therefore fails with expected single matching bean but found 2. Inject Map<String,List<SyncToolSpecification>> and assert over ALL of them (no list may hold an ungated handler; the union must equal the declared surface) - that also makes a future third list fail the test instead of silently opening a hole. Denials are returned as CallToolResult(content, isError=true, null, Map.of(layer, code)) - the protocols own advisory-error shape, which a model can act on, rather than a thrown exception that surfaces as a retryable transport fault.

title: T5 roster mechanism: delegate-then-filter installed into the SDK requestHandlers map (durable core + disposable adapter)
rationale: MCP Java SDK 2.0.0 has NO supported per-caller tools/list seam (10-agent investigation 2026-07-29, javap-verified, adversarially re-checked; upstream fix = java-sdk #578 ToolsRepository, targeted 2.1, unreleased). Chosen over: stateless-handler decorator (public-API-only but switches the whole protocol variant), transport-layer response rewrite (re-implements JSON-RPC+SSE parsing at HTTP layer), and descope-to-2.1. Shape: ToolRosterFilter = durable core owning all semantics/tests (one bulk allowAll, booleans paired with ToolRegistry order BY INDEX, omit-only, uniform for human/agent); RosterFilterInstaller = disposable SmartInitializingSingleton doing two setAccessible field reads (provider.sessionFactory -> DefaultMcpStreamableServerSessionFactory.requestHandlers, package-private) and wrapping the tools/list entry once pre-traffic; smoke check FAILS STARTUP on drift. Hard prerequisites: spring.ai.mcp.server.protocol=STREAMABLE explicit (absent = legacy SSE transport, POST /mcp 404s) and a replaced transport-provider bean with an identity-carrying contextExtractor (stock default = EMPTY McpTransportContext = silent un-filter; guarded ActorClaimWiringCheck-style). Failure classes never conflated: installation fails startup; runtime roster failure degrades to UNFILTERED (never empty). Kill-switch OFF skips the adapter+smoke-check = the post-upgrade escape hatch. Migration: delete the installer when #578 ships; the core and its tests survive. Full amendment: 00-DESIGN.md §3.2 + T5 (commit b58da5f).

name: MCP handlers run INLINE on the servlet thread inside the filter chain: SecurityContextHolder works in BOTH tools/call and tools/list
description: MEASURED 2026-07-31 in the spring-ai-mcp-hello lab over real HTTP (Spring AI 2.0.0 / MCP SDK 2.0.0 / streamable transport), not inferred. A servlet Filter set a ThreadLocal and CLEARED IT IN A FINALLY (exactly what Spring Security does); a tool handler and a reflectively-wrapped tools/list handler BOTH still saw the value, on the same http-nio-*-exec-* thread as the filter. So the handler runs INSIDE chain.doFilter(), before the unwind - because Spring AI sync auto-config sets immediateExecution(true), keeping handlers inline rather than hopping to boundedElastic. CONSEQUENCES: (1) SecurityContextHolder-based authorization works on the MCP surface for both the call and list paths - no McpTransportContext plumbing, no custom contextExtractor, no transport-provider replacement needed; (2) request-scoped state works too (RequestContextHolder), so a request-attribute-backed memo like TurnScopedCapabilityCache functions unchanged on the list path; (3) ONE identity source serves both paths, so a roster and a call gate can never disagree about the caller. FRAGILITY: this rests on immediateExecution(true); if a future Spring AI changed it, BOTH paths would lose the subject together and both fail closed (deny) - a safe, consistent failure. HOW TO RE-VERIFY after an upgrade: the lab test spring-ai-mcp-hello/src/test/.../ThreadLocalSurvivalTest + RosterFilterSpikeTest print the filter thread vs handler thread and the observed value. NOTE the anti-pattern this replaces: a gate test that calls handler.apply(null, request) on the test thread with the context set by hand proves NOTHING about the transport - the sibling repo had exactly that and no tools/call-over-HTTP test at all.

A Spring Security chain that is STATELESS and ends in anyRequest().authenticated() DENIES the ASYNC re-dispatch of any STREAMING response. Hit on example-mcp-server the moment spring.ai.mcp.server.protocol=STREAMABLE was set (T5, 2026-07-31): the MCP streamable transport answers tools/list by writing SSE, which puts the request into async mode; the AbacFilter populated the SecurityContext on the INITIAL dispatch only, so on the async re-dispatch there is no Authentication and authorizeHttpRequests denies. Because the response has already begun, the denial is NOT a clean 403 — it aborts a half-written chunked body, and the client sees 'java.io.IOException: chunked transfer encoding, state: READING_LENGTH'. Nothing in the server log says 'denied' at the point of failure; you have to read past the (unrelated, expected) degradation WARNs to find 'AuthorizationDeniedException: Access Denied' logged by the dispatcherServlet AFTER the handler completed successfully. Sibling services (catalog, user-mgmt) never hit this because they stream nothing — they only permit DispatcherType.ERROR.
resolution: Permit ASYNC alongside ERROR: .dispatcherTypeMatchers(DispatcherType.ASYNC, DispatcherType.ERROR).permitAll(). This widens nothing — an ASYNC dispatch can only exist for a request that already passed the chain on its initial dispatch, which is the same reasoning that already permits ERROR. Diagnostic tell: a wire test that gets a transport-level IOException (not a 4xx) on a streaming endpoint while the handler's own logs show it completed. A 401-before-routing test can NEVER catch this — you need a real authenticated request through the streaming endpoint.

name: MCP handler that needs request identity: decide EAGERLY on the servlet thread, apply LAZILY to the Mono
description: An MCP SDK request handler returns Mono<T>, so anything written inside .map() runs at SUBSCRIPTION time. Identity (SecurityContextHolder) and turn-scoped state (RequestContextHolder) are only provably in scope while the handler METHOD is executing. The 2026-07-31 lab spike measured that the handler does run inline on the servlet thread (Spring AI's sync auto-config sets immediateExecution(true)), but building the feature on that measurement makes it depend on an unwritten scheduling detail that a minor upgrade can change silently — and the failure mode is a SILENT feature-off (no identity -> the documented degradation path -> everyone sees everything), not a crash. The shape that removes the dependency: resolve the whole decision first, in the handler body, then return delegate.handle(...).map(result -> apply(decision, result)) where apply() is a PURE function of a plain value. Same rule applies to any outbound HTTP the decision needs (a ceiling lookup, a capability lookup, the OPA batch) — those also read request-scoped memos. Implemented as ToolRosterFilter.decide() (thread-bound) + static ToolRosterFilter.apply() (pure), wired by RosterFilterInstaller.RosterFilteringHandler.

A 'type-level ceiling' resolved by asking /internal/governed-targets for the REQUESTED resource type UNDER-approximates in this repo's model, and the failure is silent. Since slice B4 (ADR 0018) membership — and therefore the role definition — is recorded on the GOVERNING ROOT (catalog), while the role it resolves to carries permissions for the WHOLE hierarchy (a demo-editor on a catalog grants catalog+category+product actions). So governed-targets?resourceType=product returns [] for a principal who may read every product under a catalog they govern. example-mcp-server's TypeLevelRoleDefinitionSupplier (T4) did exactly this, contradicting its own class javadoc ('under-approximating would be the dangerous direction'). Two consequences, both only visible on the rig: (1) the MCP tool surface REMOVED access the same token has over REST — get_product denied at tool-gate for a human the catalog service would have served; (2) it ERASED the slice's headline, because with the human's own ceiling empty for product, an agent's get_product denial proved nothing about agent narrowing — principal and agent were denied for the same reason. Unit tests cannot catch it: they inject a synthetic RoleDefinition and never exercise the governed-targets fan-out.
resolution: Enumerate governed targets over the requested type PLUS a configurable grant-scope list (example.mcp.authz.role-source.grant-scope-types, default [catalog] — this demo's governing root), union all resolved roles, then extract permissions[requestedType] as before. Over-approximating is sound and is what the class already declared safe: the tool-gate is not the authority on resources, and the ceiling term exists only to stop an agent capability widening past the human. DIAGNOSTIC TELL: a roster that is IDENTICAL for a human and a narrowed agent, where the design says the human's should be wider. Check the ceiling before suspecting the policy.

description: Spring AI's annotation-scanned @McpTool call handler CATCHES whatever the tool method throws and flattens it into a CallToolResult with isError=true and a plain-text body ('Error invoking method: getCatalog\n...'). A wrapper around the SyncToolSpecification's callHandler therefore NEVER sees the exception: any structured detail the tool body raised (an error code, an enforcement-layer label) is gone by the time the wrapper regains control. In example-mcp-server this made a TARGET-GATE denial arrive indistinguishable from a transport fault — destroying the exact tool-gate-vs-target-gate distinction the slice exists to demonstrate. The unit test for it (I14) PASSED throughout, because its fixture builds the SyncToolSpecification itself with a raw lambda that throws straight through; only a real denial on the rig, through the real annotation-scanned handler, exposed it. Same class of gap as a tools/list test that never exercises real routing.
resolution: Carry the structured detail across the swallowing seam out-of-band: a request-scoped holder (ToolFailureRecord, backed by RequestContextHolder attributes — one tools/call is one request, so it dies naturally) written at the client's throw site and read by the gate AFTER the delegate returns. The gate relabels only a result that is ALREADY isError, so it can never turn an error into a success, and a lost record degrades to a generic advisory. REGRESSION-TEST RULE: when testing a wrapper around a third-party-built handler, the fixture must reproduce the third party's INVOCATION CONTRACT (here: a delegate that swallows), not a convenient hand-built one — otherwise the test pins a path production never takes.

name: Fault-injectable per-edge HTTP client: own breaker, own base-URL property (default to the PROPERTY not the env var), empty-from-the-body
description: Adding a SECOND cross-service HTTP edge to an app that already has one (SUPERVISED-SCOPE T4: /internal/supervised-targets beside /internal/effective-role and /internal/tag-definitions) has three non-obvious shape requirements beyond copying the shipped client. (1) OWN CallGuard instance, never a shared one: reusing resolveCallGuard means an outage on the NEW endpoint trips the breaker every persona's role resolution depends on, converting a narrow degrade (this feature falls back) into a total one (everyone gets an empty page). Build it from the same resilience.resolve.* budget but as a separate Resilience4jCallGuard bean with its own @Qualifier. (2) OWN base-URL property, and its default must reference the PROPERTY, not the environment variable. '\''supervised-base-url: ${NEW_ENV:${OLD_ENV:http://localhost:8080}}'\'' LOOKS equivalent to defaulting to the shared base-url and is not: with OLD_ENV unset - every test context, and any deployment that sets the shared URL by any other mechanism - the new edge silently falls back to localhost while the rest of the service goes elsewhere. The symptom is a permanently degraded feature with no error, only a WARN. Correct form: '\''${NEW_ENV:${catalog.user-service.base-url}}'\''. The reason to split the property at all is FAULT INJECTION: an e2e outage case must fault ONE edge, and the shipped B3 mechanism (ENABLE_RESILIENCE_STUB=1) repoints the whole user-service the rest of the matrix needs.
